title: FUTON: Fourier Tensor Networks for Implicit Neural Representations
claim: A signal is computed by expanding each input axis in a fixed basis, combining the expansions with low-rank learned factors, then decoding with a small head.
layout: 4 panels, left-to-right, numbered stages with formulas beneath each
description: A wide four-column figure read left to right. On the left, an input photo of a gold-crowned statue holding a golden sphere has dashed green and blue lines marking pixel coordinates x1 and x2. Three numbered panels follow. (1) Basis expansion: each axis passes through stacked cosine curves, sampled at the coordinate to give a colored vector φ(x). (2) Tensor-network combiner: factor matrices U(1) and U(2) (heatmaps in purple-to-orange) produce vectors h1 and h2, which are multiplied elementwise (⊙) into g(x). (3) Head: a small MLP with ReLU and tanh outputs R, G and B, and the result is compared with the true pixel colour. Green and blue are used for the two axes. Each panel has a title, a subtitle and a formula at the bottom, e.g. g(x) = ⊙ U^T φ(x_c).
caption: FUTON's forward pass for one pixel of an image ($C = 2$, $D = 3$). (1) A fixed basis, here cosines, expands each coordinate $x_c$ into $K_c$ functions, at spectral resolution $K = (K_1, K_2)$. (2) The combiner's factor matrices $\mtx{U}^{(c)}$ project each expansion onto $R$ components, multiplied across axes into $\vct{g}(\vct{x})$: a CP decomposition of the coefficient tensor. (3) A learned head, here an MLP, maps $\vct{g}(\vct{x})$ to the signal. Arrays hold exact values for random factors, at sizes far below practice.
abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) have emerged as powerful tools for encoding signals, yet dominant MLP-based designs often suffer from slow convergence, and how their accuracy depends on their size is known only empirically. We introduce FUTON (Fourier Tensor Network), which models signals as generalized Fourier series whose coefficients are parameterized by a low-rank tensor decomposition, read out by a linear or MLP head. FUTON combines complementary inductive biases: Fourier bases capture smoothness and periodicity, while the low-rank parameterization enforces low-dimensional spectral structure. Beyond universal approximation, we show that with a linear head, the best FUTON's error splits exactly into the truncation of the signal's series and the best low-rank error of its coefficients, which we bracket from the samples before training, with a FUTON that attains the upper bound. On image fitting, occupancy volumes, and novel view synthesis, against twelve INRs of matched size, FUTON achieves the best average quality, reaches the final quality of each task's strongest baseline 4-34x sooner than that baseline, infers fastest, and trains in the least memory.
